experiment.title: Rhodopsin cell surface trafficking MAVE (Method 1 & 2)
experiment.shortDescription: A Deep Mutational Scan to identify all trafficking defect variants in rhodopsin.
experiment.abstractText: This experiment evaluates every rhodopsin missense amino acid variant to determine which variants misfold and fail to traffic to the cell surface,
experiment.methodText: A saturation mutagenesis library encoding all possible single amino acid substitutions in human RHO was introduced into heterologous cells and assessed using complementary high-throughput trafficking assays. In the first assay, cell-surface rhodopsin expression was quantified by antibody staining and fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), followed by next-generation sequencing of the ORF. In the second assay, variants were integrated as single copy into landing-pad cells and evaluated using a membrane proximity transcriptional reporter.  The RNA barcodes were quantified by sequencing. In both approaches, normalized scores quantify the relative effects of rhodopsin variants on protein folding, intracellular trafficking, and cell-surface localization compared with wild-type rhodopsin. In both approaches, normalized scores measure the trafficking and cell-surface expression of RHO variants relative to wild type.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: A comprehensive map of missense trafficking variants in rhodopsin and their response to pharmacologic correction
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Rhodopsin (RHO) missense variants are a leading cause of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa (adRP), a progressive retinal degeneration with no currently approved therapies. Interpreting the pathogenicity of the growing number of identifiedRHOvariants is a major clinical challenge, and understanding their disease mechanisms is essential for developing effective therapies. Here, we present a high-resolution map ofRHOmissense variant trafficking using two complementary deep mutational scanning (DMS) approaches based on a surface abundance immunoassay and a membrane proximity assay. We generated a comprehensive dataset encompassing all 6,612 possible single-residue missense variants, revealing a strong correlation between the two methods. Over 700 variants were identified with pathogenic trafficking scores, significantly expanding the number ofRHOvariants with functional evidence supporting pathogenicity. We demonstrate a high concordance between the trafficking scores and ClinVar pathogenicity classifications, highlighting this approach’s utility in resolving variants of uncertain significance (VUS). The data also identified structurally clustered trafficking-deficient variants, predominantly within the N-terminal region and second extracellular loop, in and above the extracellular/intradiscal beta-plug region. experiment.methodText: A saturation mutagenesis library encoding all possible single amino acid substitutions in human RHO was introduced into heterologous cells and assessed using complementary high-throughput trafficking assays. In the first assay, cell-surface rhodopsin expression was quantified by antibody staining and fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), followed by next-generation sequencing of the ORF. In both approaches, normalized scores quantify the relative effects of rhodopsin variants on protein folding, intracellular trafficking, and cell-surface localization compared with wild-type rhodopsin. In both approaches, normalized scores measure the trafficking and cell-surface expression of RHO variants relative to wild type.

experiment.title: Site-saturation functional screen of PALB2 missense variants in mES cells
experiment.shortDescription: Site-saturation fuctional screen of PALB2 missense variants in the CC and WD40 domains in mouse embryonic stem cells using PARPi sensitivity as a readout for homologous recombination
experiment.abstractText: Loss-of-function variants in _PALB2_ give rise to defects in DNA damage repair by homologous recombination (HR), increasing the risk of breast cancer in female carriers. However, genetic testing frequently reveals missense variants of uncertain significance (VUS) for which the impact on protein function and cancer risk are unclear. Here we assay 84% of all possible missense variants in 11 out of 13 _PALB2_ exons using site-saturation functional screens with PARP inhibitor sensitivity as a readout for HR. These exons encode the coiled-coil and WD40 domains, which we identify as the minimal regions required for HR. Furthermore, we reveal the functional impact of 6718 missense variants, classifying 3904 variants as functional (58%), 2422 as intermediate (36%), and 392 as damaging (6%). A burden-type analysis shows that damaging missense variants in _PALB2_ are associated with a significantly increased risk of breast cancer, similar to that observed for truncating variants. These results will be valuable for the classification of _PALB2_ missense VUS and clinical management of carriers.
experiment.methodText: A cDNA-based site-saturation screen was used to measure _PALB2_ function via PARPi sensitivity as a readout for homologous recombination. Palb2-knockout mouse embryonic stem cells were used to express _PALB2_ cDNA variant libraries which were at the Rosa26 locus via recombination-mediated cassette exchange. Cells expressing _PALB2_ variants were treated with PARP inhibitor (olaparib), and next-generation sequencing was used to determine the frequency of each variant in treated vs. untreated conditions. Depletion scores were generated using Enrich2.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Comprehensive analysis of the functional impact of single nucleotide variants of human CHEK2.
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Loss of function mutations in the checkpoint kinase gene CHEK2 are associated with increased risk of breast and other cancers. Most of the 3,188 unique amino acid changes that can result from non-synonymous single nucleotide variants (SNVs) of CHEK2, however, have not been tested for their impact on the function of the CHEK2-enocded protein (CHK2). One successful approach to testing the function of variants has been to test for their ability to complement mutations in the yeast ortholog of CHEK2, RAD53. This approach has been used to provide functional information on over 100 CHEK2 SNVs and the results align with functional assays in human cells and known pathogenicity. Here we tested all but two of the 4,887 possible SNVs in the CHEK2 open reading frame for their ability to complement RAD53 mutants using a high throughput technique of deep mutational scanning (DMS). Among the non-synonymous changes, 770 were damaging to protein function while 2,417 were tolerated. The results correlate well with previous structure and function data and provide a first or additional functional assay for all the variants of uncertain significance identified in clinical databases. Combined, this approach can be used to help predict the pathogenicity of CHEK2 variants of uncertain significance that are found in susceptibility screening and could be applied to other cancer risk genes.

experiment.title: A Functional Genetic Atlas of Parkin Resolves Variants of Uncertain Significance and Predicts Parkinson’s Disease Age at Onset
experiment.shortDescription: A near-complete MAVE of the Parkin E3 ubiquitin ligase (PRKN), measuring the impact of ~9,200 missense and nonsense variants on phosphorylated ubiquitin (pSer65-Ub) accumulation and Parkin abundance following mitochondrial depolarisation in HeLa cells.
experiment.abstractText: Autosomal recessive mutations in the Parkin gene (PRKN) cause early-onset Parkinson’s disease (PD). Parkin functions as a ubiquitin E3 ligase acting downstream of the PINK1 kinase to promote phosphorylated ubiquitin at sites of mitochondrial damage. Yet the functional effects of most PRKN gene variants remain unknown. Here we use a pooled cellular assay measuring phosphorylated ubiquitin accumulation to quantify the activity of ~9,200 PRKN missense and nonsense variants. Our screen identifies thousands of loss- and gain-of-function variants, including activating variants mainly residing at autoinhibitory interfaces. Functional scores accurately distinguish known PD pathogenic and benign variants, and enable reclassification of 173/184 variants of uncertain significance (VUS). When combined into biallelic genotype scores, these data predict the age at disease onset in patients, revealing a quantitative link between Parkin activity and clinical manifestation. Our results provide a comprehensive functional genetic map of Parkin and demonstrate the power of MAVEs for variant interpretation and precision medicine in PD.
experiment.methodText:
A saturation mutagenesis library covering 9,234 of 9,280 possible single missense and nonsense variants of human PRKN was generated by nicking mutagenesis using NNS/NNK degenerate oligonucleotides. Each variant was linked to a unique 30-nucleotide barcode via Gateway LR recombination into a barcoded destination vector. Barcode-variant linkage was established by PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing processed with alignparse. 

The barcoded library was integrated into HeLa cells carrying a single genomic BxB1 recombinase landing pad by electroporation, followed by two weeks of puromycin selection to maintain single genomic integrants. Two parallel pooled screens were performed on the same cell library.

In the activity screen, cells were treated with 1 µM oligomycin A and 10 µM antimycin A (OA) for 45 minutes to induce mitochondrial depolarisation and PINK1-dependent Parkin activation, then fixed, permeabilised in 90% methanol, and stained with a monoclonal anti-pSer65-Ub antibody. In the abundance screen, cells were treated with OA under identical conditions, then fixed and permeabilised and stained with a monoclonal anti-Parkin antibody. In both screens, cells were sorted by FACS into four bins based on fluorescence intensity (≥10 million cells per bin), and genomic DNA was extracted by phenol-chloroform extraction.

Barcodes were amplified by PCR with Illumina P5/P7 primers, and sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq platform. Reads were aligned to the PacBio barcode library using Enrich2 and variant scores were computed as the weighted average barcode distribution across bins, excluding barcodes with fewer than 150 total reads. False discovery rates were calculated by bootstrapping against wild-type and stop-codon barcodes. Both screens were performed as single pooled experiments with no library-scale biological replicates. Raw sequencing data and processed barcode count files are deposited in GEO (accession GSE335967); analysis scripts are available at https://zenodo.org/records/20782756.

experiment.title: A Functional Genetic Atlas of Parkin Resolves Variants of Uncertain Significance and Predicts Parkinson’s Disease Age at Onset
experiment.shortDescription: A near-complete MAVE of the Parkin E3 ubiquitin ligase (PRKN), measuring the impact of ~9,200 missense and nonsense variants on phosphorylated ubiquitin (pSer65-Ub) accumulation and Parkin abundance following mitochondrial depolarisation in HeLa cells.
experiment.abstractText: Autosomal recessive mutations in the Parkin gene (PRKN) cause early-onset Parkinson’s disease (PD). Parkin functions as a ubiquitin E3 ligase acting downstream of the PINK1 kinase to promote phosphorylated ubiquitin at sites of mitochondrial damage. Yet the functional effects of most PRKN gene variants remain unknown. Here we use a pooled cellular assay measuring phosphorylated ubiquitin accumulation to quantify the activity of ~9,200 PRKN missense and nonsense variants. Our screen identifies thousands of loss- and gain-of-function variants, including activating variants mainly residing at autoinhibitory interfaces. Functional scores accurately distinguish known PD pathogenic and benign variants, and enable reclassification of 173/184 variants of uncertain significance (VUS). When combined into biallelic genotype scores, these data predict the age at disease onset in patients, revealing a quantitative link between Parkin activity and clinical manifestation. Our results provide a comprehensive functional genetic map of Parkin and demonstrate the power of MAVEs for variant interpretation and precision medicine in PD.
experiment.methodText:
A saturation mutagenesis library covering 9,234 of 9,280 possible single missense and nonsense variants of human PRKN was generated by nicking mutagenesis using NNS/NNK degenerate oligonucleotides. Each variant was linked to a unique 30-nucleotide barcode via Gateway LR recombination into a barcoded destination vector. Barcode-variant linkage was established by PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing processed with alignparse. 

The barcoded library was integrated into HeLa cells carrying a single genomic BxB1 recombinase landing pad by electroporation, followed by two weeks of puromycin selection to maintain single genomic integrants. Two parallel pooled screens were performed on the same cell library.

In the activity screen, cells were treated with 1 µM oligomycin A and 10 µM antimycin A (OA) for 45 minutes to induce mitochondrial depolarisation and PINK1-dependent Parkin activation, then fixed, permeabilised in 90% methanol, and stained with a monoclonal anti-pSer65-Ub antibody. In the abundance screen, cells were treated with OA under identical conditions, then fixed and permeabilised and stained with a monoclonal anti-Parkin antibody. In both screens, cells were sorted by FACS into four bins based on fluorescence intensity (≥10 million cells per bin), and genomic DNA was extracted by phenol-chloroform extraction.

Barcodes were amplified by PCR with Illumina P5/P7 primers, and sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq platform. Reads were aligned to the PacBio barcode library using Enrich2 and variant scores were computed as the weighted average barcode distribution across bins, excluding barcodes with fewer than 150 total reads. False discovery rates were calculated by bootstrapping against wild-type and stop-codon barcodes. Both screens were performed as single pooled experiments with no library-scale biological replicates. Raw sequencing data and processed barcode count files are deposited in GEO (accession GSE335967); analysis scripts are available at https://zenodo.org/records/20782756.

scoreSets.shortDescription: Missense variant effect map for human CPOX via functional complementation in yeast.

experiment.title: Environment-dependent landscapes of coding variant impacts on CPOX
experiment.shortDescription: We systematically assessed CPOX variant functions with and without mercury, which can increase the penetrance of CPOX variants. By combining comprehensive codon mutagenesis with large-scale multiplexed functional assays, we experimentally measured the impacts of nearly all possible CPOX missense variants.
experiment.abstractText: Hereditary coproporphyria (HCP) — caused by variants in coproporphyrinogen oxidase (CPOX) — can be diagnosed via genome sequencing. However, 74% of clinically-reported CPOX missense variants are classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS) due to lack of evidence. CPOX variant classification is further complicated by environment-dependence: For example, the CPOX variant p.Asn272His (c.814A>C) is classified as benign yet has been associated with HCP-like symptoms in the context of mercury exposure. Here we measured the functional impact of nearly all possible CPOX amino acid substitutions in both the presence and absence of mercury. The resulting CPOX variant effect maps reflect known protein structure and mutational tolerance patterns while also offering new sequence-structure-function insights. Scores from this atlas not only distinguish pathogenic from benign variants but also identify mercury-dependent variant impacts, thus informing our clinical, structural, and functional understanding of CPOX deficiency and illustrating the value of systematic context-dependent multiplexed assays of genetic variant effects.
experiment.methodText: Scores were generated from raw data using the tileseqMut and tileseqMave pipelines. For a variant to be included in the score set, a minimum of 10 reads per variant were necessary in the non-select condition. The scores were scaled to 0 and 1 based on the centered distributions of the nonsense and synonymous scores, respectively. Biological replicate scores were averaged and error calculated using an inverse-variance weighted average of scores, with weights proportional to the combined standard deviation computed from the weighted variances and degrees of freedom. Use of inverse-variance weighted averages provided greater weights for scores with lower uncertainty. For variants with no replicate, the standard error and ‘degrees of freedom’ were taken directly from the existing biological replicate. Score columns include the variant (hgvs_pro), the functional score, standard error of score (se), degrees of freedom (df), log-likelihood ratios of pathogenicity (LLRp), and the conversion of LLRps to ACMG-compatible evidence strengths (evidence_weight). LLRp confidence intervals can be found in the supplemental manuscript files.

scoreSets.title: SGCA variants effects on α-sarcoglycan surface expression
scoreSets.shortDescription: SGCA variants effects on α-sarcoglycan surface expression

experiment.title: Deep Mutational Scanning in SGCA with Saturation Mutagenesis-Reinforced Functional Assays (SMuRF)
experiment.shortDescription: Comprehensive functional assessment of all possible coding single-nucleotide variants in SGCA using saturation mutagenesis and a cell-surface localization assay.
experiment.abstractText: Pathogenic variants in SGCA, encoding α-sarcoglycan, cause an autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, LGMDR3/2D, yet clinical interpretation of SGCA variants remains challenging due to the high prevalence of rare missense variants. α-sarcoglycan is an essential component of the sarcoglycan complex at the muscle cell membrane, and pathogenic variants frequently impair its membrane localization. Here, we systematically assess the effects of all possible single-nucleotide variants across the SGCA coding sequence using a saturation mutagenesis-based experimental assay that quantifies α-sarcoglycan surface expression. We generate a comprehensive functional atlas that distinguishes tolerated and damaging variants, aligning with independent genetic and clinical evidence, and reveals domain-specific properties of the cytoplasmic region, in which C-terminal truncating variants retain membrane localization, suggesting possible pathogenic mechanisms beyond impaired trafficking. This work provides a scalable functional framework to support genetic diagnosis and variant interpretation in sarcoglycanopathies.
experiment.methodText:
Saturation Mutagenesis-Reinforced Functional Assays (SMuRF) is an accessible workflow for deep mutational scanning (DMS) studies. The manuscript is currently in preparation. This workflow involves a 2-way extension PCR-based saturation mutagenesis and high-throughput functional assays that can be evaluated with short-read Next-generation sequencing.  

For SGCA, all possible coding single-nucleotide variants were generated across five non-overlapping mutagenesis blocks. Variant effects were evaluated using a FACS-based assay measuring α-sarcoglycan cell-surface expression in HEK-BDG cells stably expressing β-, δ-, and γ-sarcoglycan. Surface α-sarcoglycan was detected by live-cell staining of an extracellular FLAG epitope, and cells were separated into high- and low-surface-expression populations. Variant enrichment was quantified by NGS, and membrane localization scores (MLSs) were generated from three biological replicates.  

 

We have organized scripts used for SMuRF across three repositories:  

Balthazar repository is used to create the oligo library needed for the saturation mutagenesis as well as perform QC for the resulting construct.  

Gargamel repository is used to process the raw data from NGS to quantify the enrichment of the variants.  

DeniSa repository is used to generate and analyze the membrane localization scores (MLSs), SMuRF scores, process the nonsense variant library, analyze clinical data, and plot the results.

scoreSets.shortDescription: SGE of exons 4, 5 and 6 of TINF2.

experiment.title: Functional mapping and pedigree-based clinical analysis of cancer-associated TINF2 long-telomere variants
experiment.shortDescription: Saturation Genome Editing in HAP1 cells of TINF2. We targeted exons 4, 5 and 6, of the MANE TINF2 transcript ENST00000267415.12 (NCBI RefSeq: NM_001099274.3), corresponding to amino acid residues 134-269. The screened regions, in which systematic variation was installed, comprised: exon 4 (GRCh38: chr14:24241336-24241198), exon 5 (chr14:24241116-24241020), and exon 6 (chr14:24240813-24240673), which partially cover the TRFH-like domain and the TRFH-binding motif involved in TRF1 binding.
experiment.abstractText: Disruptive germline TINF2 variants are associated with long telomeres and familial cancer predisposition, but their functional effects and associated tumour spectrum remain poorly defined. Here, we use saturation genome editing to quantify the effects of 3,912 variants across TINF2 exons 4-6, encompassing the TRFH-like domain that mediates TRF2 and TPP1 binding and the TRFH-binding motif that mediates TRF1 binding. Predicted loss-of-function (LoF) alleles were strongly depleted, denoting gene disruption, and missense intolerance was mapped to functionally constrained shelterin-interaction domains.
experiment.methodText:
FASTQ files were converted to counts using the QUANTS pipeline for each timepoint-replicate - https://github.com/cancerit/QUANTS

Variants were annotated by VEP (https://github.com/Ensembl/ensembl-vep) and VaLiAnT (https://github.com/cancerit/valiant) meta-data outputs

Low count variants (fewer than 10 summed over all timepoint-replicates) were filter out

Normalisation matrices (synonymous and intronic variants) were created to calculate control size-factors.

DESeq2 was run with adjusted size factors to calculate raw log fold changes (LFCs) and statistics (LFC shrinkage off).

QC plots for replicate consistency, dispersion, sample correlation and editing efficiency were assessed and any poor replicates removed and DESeq2 re-run with adapted experimental conditions.

p-values were calculated using a two-tailed z-test and FDR correction of p-value performed using the BH method on total unique variants.

Functional classifications were computed from from functional score and FDR values

experiment.title: Four deep missense scans of AGXT reveal dependence on environmental and genetic context
experiment.shortDescription:
We tested AGXT variants in the background of the wild-type allele and in cis with the most common minor allele (p.Pro11Leu, p.Ile340Met).
After these two maps were completed we also re-tested these libraries in the context of Vitamin B6 supplementation, because PLP is the cofactor of the protein and recommended to patients.
experiment.abstractText: The human alanine glyoxylate aminotransferase (AGT) enzyme, encoded by the gene AGXT, plays a crucial role in liver glycine metabolism. Although glycine is a nonessential amino acid, AGT dysfunction causes several renal diseases, including primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (PH1). Nearly 20% of clinical AGXT missense variants are classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS), limiting opportunities for diagnosis and therapy. Supplementation with vitamin B6 (VB6) can lessen PH1 severity for patients with some variants, but not for others. For some variants, appearance in cis with a common minor (“*2”) allele increases PH1 severity. Here we measured the function of nearly all possible AGT amino acid substitutions based on their ability to rescue growth of a Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain lacking the AGXT ortholog AGX1. This was carried out in both the reference and *2 allele context, and at two vitamin B6 levels, collectively yielding four AGT ‘missense variant effect maps’. Of 7820 possible missense amino acid substitutions, 6606 (84.5%) were scored in all four contexts. The resulting atlas identifies AGXT variants for which functional impact is altered by a common genetic background or by cofactor treatment, provides evidentiary resource for identifying pathogenic AGXT missense variants.
experiment.methodText: Yeast lacking SHM1, SHM2, AGX1 and GLY1 can not grow media without glycine. Variants of AGXT were made, integrated into destination vectors with gateway cloning and yeast transformation and transformant selection followed. A 7-9 days fitness selection of pooled transformed cells in media deficient in glycine was conducted. Pre-selection and post-selection variant pools were extracted, tiled and sequencing with short-read Illumina adapters. Ratio of variant frequencies were calculated as log(phi) and fitness scores were calculated considering WT reference, nonsense and synonimous distributions.

experiment.methodText: The WT-relative score (see the paired raw score set) is divided by a per-replicate standard-curve slope fit to spiked BRAF-variant standards of known effect size, putting every library, assay, and treatment arm on one common, standardized scale before averaging over replicates. Score columns: score = mean standardized effect size across replicates (on this scale, unlike the raw score, a shift in wild type itself between treatment arms is preserved rather than re-anchored to 1); standardized_score_replicate_1-3 = the standardized score in each individual replicate. mentions the included BRAF standard-control variants; empty_vector_std (no ORF, no protein product) is represented as BRAF:p.Met1_His766del, a full-length deletion of BRAF specifically (not the host protein), so it reads as the same control across every dataset.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Massively scaled variant effect mapping across the MAPK pathway reveals the importance of molecular and cellular context
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Variation alters inherent protein properties like thermodynamic stability and catalytic activity, and these intrinsic effects are shaped by the complex cellular environment. Signaling cascades typify this complexity, with tens or hundreds of proteins acting in concert through regulated states and interactions to transduce signals. Here, we measure the effect of 186,676 variants across 17 proteins in the RAS-MAPK pathway on protein abundance and pathway activity in human cells under diverse conditions, for a total of 503,099 variant effect measurements. We discovered 14,412 dominant negative variants across 12 proteins, nearly all previously unknown, that disrupt specific domains or interaction interfaces while leaving other functions intact and that are depleted from the human population. Measuring the abundance of 106,642 variants across 10 proteins under HSP90 inhibition showed that HSP90 shapes the effect of 67% of missense variants across the pathway, buffering destabilizing variants in both strong and weak clients. Our variant effect data, collected in the context of an intact proteome, enabled us to assess the functional importance of 395 experimentally and computationally modeled MAPK protein interactions. Using additional mutational scans, we resolved how the promiscuous switch II helix binding surface of KRAS accommodates overlapping interactions with LZTR1 and SOS1, revealing distinct allosteric networks that support each interaction. Thus, we establish a framework for measuring variant effects at unprecedented scale in human cells, illuminating fundamental MAPK pathway signaling mechanisms and demonstrating that cellular context profoundly shapes the effect of most variants.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Massively scaled variant effect mapping across the MAPK pathway reveals the importance of molecular and cellular context
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Variation alters inherent protein properties like thermodynamic stability and catalytic activity, and these intrinsic effects are shaped by the complex cellular environment. Signaling cascades typify this complexity, with tens or hundreds of proteins acting in concert through regulated states and interactions to transduce signals. Here, we measure the effect of 186,676 variants across 17 proteins in the RAS-MAPK pathway on protein abundance and pathway activity in human cells under diverse conditions, for a total of 503,099 variant effect measurements. We discovered 14,412 dominant negative variants across 12 proteins, nearly all previously unknown, that disrupt specific domains or interaction interfaces while leaving other functions intact and that are depleted from the human population. Measuring the abundance of 106,642 variants across 10 proteins under HSP90 inhibition showed that HSP90 shapes the effect of 67% of missense variants across the pathway, buffering destabilizing variants in both strong and weak clients. Our variant effect data, collected in the context of an intact proteome, enabled us to assess the functional importance of 395 experimentally and computationally modeled MAPK protein interactions. Using additional mutational scans, we resolved how the promiscuous switch II helix binding surface of KRAS accommodates overlapping interactions with LZTR1 and SOS1, revealing distinct allosteric networks that support each interaction. Thus, we establish a framework for measuring variant effects at unprecedented scale in human cells, illuminating fundamental MAPK pathway signaling mechanisms and demonstrating that cellular context profoundly shapes the effect of most variants.

Here, we measure the effect of 186,676 variants across 17 proteins in the RAS-MAPK pathway on protein abundance and pathway activity in human cells under diverse conditions, for a total of 503,099 variant effect measurements. We discovered 14,412 dominant negative variants across 12 proteins, nearly all previously unknown, that disrupt specific domains or interaction interfaces while leaving other functions intact and that are depleted from the human population. Measuring the abundance of 106,642 variants across 10 proteins under HSP90 inhibition showed that HSP90 shapes the effect of 67% of missense variants across the pathway, buffering destabilizing variants in both strong and weak clients. Our variant effect data, collected in the context of an intact proteome, enabled us to assess the functional importance of 395 experimentally and computationally modeled MAPK protein interactions. Using additional mutational scans, we resolved how the promiscuous switch II helix binding surface of KRAS accommodates overlapping interactions with LZTR1 and SOS1, revealing distinct allosteric networks that support each interaction. Thus, we establish a framework for measuring variant effects at unprecedented scale in human cells, illuminating fundamental MAPK pathway signaling mechanisms and demonstrating that cellular context profoundly shapes the effect of most variants.

experiment.title: ERBB2 activity — baseline
experiment.shortDescription: ERBB2 WT-relative variant effects on MAPK pathway activity (ERK2 phosphorylation), from the LABEL-seq MAPK pathway atlas.
experiment.abstractText: Variant-effect measurements of ERBB2 from LABEL-seq, a barcode-sequencing assay that converts MAPK pathway activity (ERK2 phosphorylation) into a sequencing-based readout in human cells. Part of a 17-protein, pathway-scale atlas of MAPK/ERK signaling variant effects.
experiment.methodText: ERBB2 variant libraries were expressed in human cells together with a co-expressed circular-RNA barcode (LABEL-seq); pathway activity was reported as the ratio of barcode enrichment by phosphorylated vs. unphosphorylated tdMCP-ERK2. Three biological replicates were sequenced per condition (two for the interaction assay). Every library included internal BRAF-derived standard-curve variants spanning a known range of effect sizes. Variant libraries were constructed by svClone (synthetic DNA variant cloning); full protocols are in the associated publication. mentions the included BRAF standard-control variants; empty_vector_std (no ORF, no protein product) is represented as BRAF:p.Met1_His766del, a full-length deletion of BRAF specifically (not the host protein), so it reads as the same control across every dataset.

experiment.title: MET abundance — DMSO (standardized)
experiment.shortDescription: MET standardized variant effects on protein abundance under vehicle (DMSO) treatment, from the LABEL-seq MAPK pathway atlas.
experiment.abstractText: Variant-effect measurements of MET from LABEL-seq, a barcode-sequencing assay that converts protein abundance into a sequencing-based readout in human cells under vehicle (DMSO) treatment. Part of a 17-protein, pathway-scale atlas of MAPK/ERK signaling variant effects.
experiment.methodText: The WT-relative score (see the paired raw score set) is divided by a per-replicate standard-curve slope fit to spiked BRAF-variant standards of known effect size, putting every library, assay, and treatment arm on one common, standardized scale before averaging over replicates. Score columns: score = mean standardized effect size across replicates (on this scale, unlike the raw score, a shift in wild type itself between treatment arms is preserved rather than re-anchored to 1); standardized_score_replicate_1-3 = the standardized score in each individual replicate. mentions the included BRAF standard-control variants; empty_vector_std (no ORF, no protein product) is represented as BRAF:p.Met1_His766del, a full-length deletion of BRAF specifically (not the host protein), so it reads as the same control across every dataset. this cell was sequenced twice (MET is the only one) and both runs are pooled into one record -- a barcode observed in both runs is counted twice by design, not a duplicate to be collapsed.

experiment.title: RET abundance — HSP90i (standardized)
experiment.shortDescription: RET standardized variant effects on protein abundance under HSP90 inhibition (pimitespib), from the LABEL-seq MAPK pathway atlas.
experiment.abstractText: Variant-effect measurements of RET from LABEL-seq, a barcode-sequencing assay that converts protein abundance into a sequencing-based readout in human cells under HSP90 inhibition (pimitespib). Part of a 17-protein, pathway-scale atlas of MAPK/ERK signaling variant effects.
experiment.methodText: The WT-relative score (see the paired raw score set) is divided by a per-replicate standard-curve slope fit to spiked BRAF-variant standards of known effect size, putting every library, assay, and treatment arm on one common, standardized scale before averaging over replicates. Score columns: score = mean standardized effect size across replicates (on this scale, unlike the raw score, a shift in wild type itself between treatment arms is preserved rather than re-anchored to 1); standardized_score_replicate_1-3 = the standardized score in each individual replicate. mentions the included BRAF standard-control variants; empty_vector_std (no ORF, no protein product) is represented as BRAF:p.Met1_His766del, a full-length deletion of BRAF specifically (not the host protein), so it reads as the same control across every dataset.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Massively scaled variant effect mapping across the MAPK pathway reveals the importance of molecular and cellular context
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Variation alters inherent protein properties like thermodynamic stability and catalytic activity, and these intrinsic effects are shaped by the complex cellular environment. Signaling cascades typify this complexity, with tens or hundreds of proteins acting in concert through regulated states and interactions to transduce signals. Here, we measure the effect of 186,676 variants across 17 proteins in the RAS-MAPK pathway on protein abundance and pathway activity in human cells under diverse conditions, for a total of 503,099 variant effect measurements. We discovered 14,412 dominant negative variants across 12 proteins, nearly all previously unknown, that disrupt specific domains or interaction interfaces while leaving other functions intact and that are depleted from the human population. Measuring the abundance of 106,642 variants across 10 proteins under HSP90 inhibition showed that HSP90 shapes the effect of 67% of missense variants across the pathway, buffering destabilizing variants in both strong and weak clients. Our variant effect data, collected in the context of an intact proteome, enabled us to assess the functional importance of 395 experimentally and computationally modeled MAPK protein interactions. Using additional mutational scans, we resolved how the promiscuous switch II helix binding surface of KRAS accommodates overlapping interactions with LZTR1 and SOS1, revealing distinct allosteric networks that support each interaction. Thus, we establish a framework for measuring variant effects at unprecedented scale in human cells, illuminating fundamental MAPK pathway signaling mechanisms and demonstrating that cellular context profoundly shapes the effect of most variants.

experiment.title: RET abundance — HSP90i
experiment.shortDescription: RET WT-relative variant effects on protein abundance under HSP90 inhibition (pimitespib), from the LABEL-seq MAPK pathway atlas.
experiment.abstractText: Variant-effect measurements of RET from LABEL-seq, a barcode-sequencing assay that converts protein abundance into a sequencing-based readout in human cells under HSP90 inhibition (pimitespib). Part of a 17-protein, pathway-scale atlas of MAPK/ERK signaling variant effects.
experiment.methodText: RET variant libraries were expressed in human cells together with a co-expressed circular-RNA barcode (LABEL-seq); protein abundance was reported as the ratio of circular-RNA barcode enrichment by a tdMCP-tagged variant to that of a stably expressed tdMCP-tagged competitor protein, under HSP90 inhibition (pimitespib). Three biological replicates were sequenced per condition (two for the interaction assay). Every library included internal BRAF-derived standard-curve variants spanning a known range of effect sizes. Variant libraries were constructed by svClone (synthetic DNA variant cloning); full protocols are in the associated publication. mentions the included BRAF standard-control variants; empty_vector_std (no ORF, no protein product) is represented as BRAF:p.Met1_His766del, a full-length deletion of BRAF specifically (not the host protein), so it reads as the same control across every dataset.

experiment.methodText: ARAF variant libraries were expressed in human cells together with a co-expressed circular-RNA barcode (LABEL-seq); protein abundance was reported as the ratio of circular-RNA barcode enrichment by a tdMCP-tagged variant to that of a stably expressed tdMCP-tagged competitor protein, under vehicle (DMSO) treatment. experiment.methodText: ARAF variant libraries were expressed in human cells together with a co-expressed circular-RNA barcode (LABEL-seq); protein abundance was reported as the ratio of circular-RNA barcode enrichment by a tdMCP-tagged variant to that of a stably expressed tdMCP-tagged competitor protein. Three biological replicates were sequenced per condition (two for the interaction assay). Every library included internal BRAF-derived standard-curve variants spanning a known range of effect sizes. Variant libraries were constructed by svClone (synthetic DNA variant cloning); full protocols are in the associated publication. mentions the included BRAF standard-control variants; empty_vector_std (no ORF, no protein product) is represented as BRAF:p.Met1_His766del, a full-length deletion of BRAF specifically (not the host protein), so it reads as the same control across every dataset.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Massively scaled variant effect mapping across the MAPK pathway reveals the importance of molecular and cellular context
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Variation alters inherent protein properties like thermodynamic stability and catalytic activity, and these intrinsic effects are shaped by the complex cellular environment. Signaling cascades typify this complexity, with tens or hundreds of proteins acting in concert through regulated states and interactions to transduce signals. Here, we measure the effect of 186,676 variants across 17 proteins in the RAS-MAPK pathway on protein abundance and pathway activity in human cells under diverse conditions, for a total of 503,099 variant effect measurements. We discovered 14,412 dominant negative variants across 12 proteins, nearly all previously unknown, that disrupt specific domains or interaction interfaces while leaving other functions intact and that are depleted from the human population. Measuring the abundance of 106,642 variants across 10 proteins under HSP90 inhibition showed that HSP90 shapes the effect of 67% of missense variants across the pathway, buffering destabilizing variants in both strong and weak clients. Our variant effect data, collected in the context of an intact proteome, enabled us to assess the functional importance of 395 experimentally and computationally modeled MAPK protein interactions. Using additional mutational scans, we resolved how the promiscuous switch II helix binding surface of KRAS accommodates overlapping interactions with LZTR1 and SOS1, revealing distinct allosteric networks that support each interaction. Thus, we establish a framework for measuring variant effects at unprecedented scale in human cells, illuminating fundamental MAPK pathway signaling mechanisms and demonstrating that cellular context profoundly shapes the effect of most variants.

experiment.title: BRAF abundance — SOS1 activation (standardized)
experiment.shortDescription: BRAF standardized variant effects on protein abundance with SOS1 activation, from the LABEL-seq MAPK pathway atlas.
experiment.abstractText: Variant-effect measurements of BRAF from LABEL-seq, a barcode-sequencing assay that converts protein abundance into a sequencing-based readout in human cells with SOS1 activation. Part of a 17-protein, pathway-scale atlas of MAPK/ERK signaling variant effects.
experiment.methodText: The WT-relative score (see the paired raw score set) is divided by a per-replicate standard-curve slope fit to spiked BRAF-variant standards of known effect size, putting every library, assay, and treatment arm on one common, standardized scale before averaging over replicates. Score columns: score = mean standardized effect size across replicates (on this scale, unlike the raw score, a shift in wild type itself between treatment arms is preserved rather than re-anchored to 1); standardized_score_replicate_1-3 = the standardized score in each individual replicate. combines braf_nterm, braf_cterm (assayed, scored, and standard-curve-fit independently) into one record. 1 variant (the wild-type marker and/or spiked BRAF standard controls) were measured independently in both constructs; their standardized scores were averaged into a single value.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Variation alters inherent protein properties like thermodynamic stability and catalytic activity, and these intrinsic effects are shaped by the complex cellular environment. experiment.methodText: The WT-relative score (see the paired raw score set) is divided by a per-replicate standard-curve slope fit to spiked BRAF-variant standards of known effect size, putting every library, assay, and treatment arm on one common, standardized scale before averaging over replicates. Measuring the abundance of 106,642 variants across 10 proteins under HSP90 inhibition showed that HSP90 shapes the effect of 67% of missense variants across the pathway, buffering destabilizing variants in both strong and weak clients. Our variant effect data, collected in the context of an intact proteome, enabled us to assess the functional importance of 395 experimentally and computationally modeled MAPK protein interactions. Using additional mutational scans, we resolved how the promiscuous switch II helix binding surface of KRAS accommodates overlapping interactions with LZTR1 and SOS1, revealing distinct allosteric networks that support each interaction. Thus, we establish a framework for measuring variant effects at unprecedented scale in human cells, illuminating fundamental MAPK pathway signaling mechanisms and demonstrating that cellular context profoundly shapes the effect of most variants.

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Massively scaled variant effect mapping across the MAPK pathway reveals the importance of molecular and cellular context
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Variation alters inherent protein properties like thermodynamic stability and catalytic activity, and these intrinsic effects are shaped by the complex cellular environment. Signaling cascades typify this complexity, with tens or hundreds of proteins acting in concert through regulated states and interactions to transduce signals. Here, we measure the effect of 186,676 variants across 17 proteins in the RAS-MAPK pathway on protein abundance and pathway activity in human cells under diverse conditions, for a total of 503,099 variant effect measurements. We discovered 14,412 dominant negative variants across 12 proteins, nearly all previously unknown, that disrupt specific domains or interaction interfaces while leaving other functions intact and that are depleted from the human population. Measuring the abundance of 106,642 variants across 10 proteins under HSP90 inhibition showed that HSP90 shapes the effect of 67% of missense variants across the pathway, buffering destabilizing variants in both strong and weak clients. Our variant effect data, collected in the context of an intact proteome, enabled us to assess the functional importance of 395 experimentally and computationally modeled MAPK protein interactions. Using additional mutational scans, we resolved how the promiscuous switch II helix binding surface of KRAS accommodates overlapping interactions with LZTR1 and SOS1, revealing distinct allosteric networks that support each interaction. Thus, we establish a framework for measuring variant effects at unprecedented scale in human cells, illuminating fundamental MAPK pathway signaling mechanisms and demonstrating that cellular context profoundly shapes the effect of most variants.
